summary: Deprecates the address translation mode of iFCP because changes in Fibre Channel made its specification incorrect and nobody used it. Address transparent mode is unaffected. It updates RFC 4172 and is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: One way of working had broken and no one used it, so this officially retires it. The other way keeps working.

questions: what is ifcp address translation mode
why was ifcp address translation mode deprecated
subtitle: Retiring an unused, outdated mode of iFCP and recording why Protocol Number 133 stays allocated.

tldr.problem: Changes to Fibre Channel made the iFCP address translation mode specification incorrect, and no known implementation used it.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC says address translation mode SHOULD NOT be implemented and SHOULD NOT be used, and that its text in RFC 4172 should be treated as Historic. Address transparent mode is left alone.
tldr.outcome: RFC 4172 stays a Proposed Standard to keep address transparent mode, and Protocol Number 133 remains allocated because pre-standard FCIP was deployed.

facts.label: Requirement on translation mode
facts.value: SHOULD NOT be implemented or used

today: RFC 6172 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 4172, and the unit metadata lists nothing that obsoletes or updates RFC 6172 itself. iFCP address translation mode is deprecated, while address transparent mode remains correctly specified.

sections.title: Two Modes of iFCP
sections.content:
The Internet Fibre Channel Protocol (iFCP), specified in RFC 4172, has two modes for handling Fibre Channel N_PORT fabric addresses, which are 24-bit N_PORT_IDs.

  • Address transparent mode is a pass-through mode that preserves the addresses.
  • Address translation mode is a Fibre Channel analog to Network Address Translation (NAT). iFCP gateways change the addresses at the boundary between Fibre Channel and the Internet, and both the source (S_ID) and destination (D_ID) addresses may be changed.

This document deprecates address translation mode because its specification has not tracked changes in Fibre Channel and because there are no known implementations.
sections.plainLanguage: One mode passes the address labels along untouched. The other swaps the labels at the border. The swapping kind is the one being retired.

sections.title: Why Translation Mode Broke
sections.content:
Address translation mode has to translate addresses embedded in transmitted data, much as NAT translates IP addresses embedded in IP packets. Fibre Channel limits embedded fabric addresses to control frames: Extended Link Services (ELSs) and FC-4 Link Services for SCSI over Fibre Channel (FCP). The translations are given in Section 7.3 of RFC 4172 and were correct for Fibre Channel as of approximately 2003.

Since then, significant changes were made to FC control frames, and these changes made Section 7.3 of RFC 4172 incorrect. Deployment also diverged from expectations: all iFCP deployments known to the authors use address transparent mode, and only for FC inter-switch links. Translation mode cannot be used for those links, because the needed translations for Switch Fabric Internal Link Services have not been specified.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules for swapping labels went out of date when the things being labeled changed. Meanwhile, everyone who actually used the system picked the other mode.

sections.title: What the Deprecation Says
sections.content:
The authors judged it prudent to deprecate the mode rather than update it, since updating would create a continuing requirement to track future changes to FC control frames for an unused protocol mode.

  • Address translation mode SHOULD NOT be implemented and SHOULD NOT be used.
  • RFC 4172 remains a Proposed Standard, in order to retain the specification of address transparent mode.
  • The RFC 4172 specification of address translation mode should be treated as Historic, as defined in RFC 2026.
sections.plainLanguage: The rule book now says: do not build or use the old swapping mode. Keep the rest of the book, because the other mode is still good.

sections.title: FCIP and Protocol Number 133
sections.content:
Protocol Number 133 was allocated for Fibre Channel and used by a pre-standard version of the Fibre Channel over IP (FCIP) protocol that put FC frames directly into IP packets. The standard FCIP protocol, RFC 3821, encapsulates FC frames in TCP and so does not use that number.

Implementations of the pre-standard version were deployed, so the number needs to remain allocated. IANA has added this document as a supplemental reference for the allocation but has not changed it.
sections.plainLanguage: An old version of a system used a special locker number. Even though the new version does not need it, some old users still do, so nobody takes the locker away.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: This document adds nothing new here. The security considerations for iFCP continue to apply, as described in Section 10 of RFC 4172.
sections.plainLanguage: The safety rules for the system stay as they were.
